description: Fall of Saigon, détente and how Cold War historians have debated who was responsible.
content_html:
The Fall of Saigon 1975

Following the withdrawal of US combat troops in March 1973, the Paris Peace Accords left South Vietnam to defend itself against a continuing North Vietnamese military campaign. The South Vietnamese government received continued US financial support but no military intervention. In early 1975, North Vietnamese forces launched a major offensive. On 30 April 1975, Saigon fell. Dramatic footage of US helicopters evacuating the last Americans from the roof of the embassy transmitted a powerful image of defeat around the world. Vietnam was reunified under communist rule as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

The legacy of the war for the USA was profound. Approximately 58,000 American soldiers had died; South Vietnam had lost far more. The conflict exposed the limits of American military power, damaged public trust in government, and produced a generation of veterans dealing with physical and psychological injuries. Congress passed the War Powers Act in 1973, requiring the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and limiting deployments to 60 days without congressional approval.

Key Fact

Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. The USA had lost approximately 58,000 soldiers in a war that ended in the victory of the side it had fought against. The War Powers Act (1973) was Congress’s direct response to the way the President had bypassed congressional approval throughout the conflict.

Détente and the Relaxation of Tensions 1969–1979

Alongside the Vietnam War, a broader shift in superpower relations was underway. Détente — the French word for “relaxation” — described a policy of managing rather than winning the Cold War through negotiation. Nixon and his National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger led this approach. In February 1972 Nixon made a landmark visit to communist China, opening diplomatic relations after more than two decades of hostility. This triangular diplomacy played the USSR against China, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split.

In May 1972, Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT I agreement, the first treaty to limit the growth of nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. The Helsinki Accords of 1975, signed by 35 nations, recognised the existing European borders established after 1945 and included a commitment to human rights that Soviet dissidents later used to challenge the Kremlin.

Détente ended abruptly in December 1979 when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to prop up a communist government. The USA boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics and Carter withdrew the SALT II treaty from Senate ratification. The invasion marked the return of intense superpower competition, sometimes called the “Second Cold War”. The episode showed how the structure of détente — based on negotiation rather than shared values — was vulnerable to a single decisive military action.

Cold War Historiography: Orthodox, Revisionist and Post-Revisionist

Historians have debated responsibility for the Cold War across three broad schools of thought. The orthodox school, dominant in the 1950s and 1960s, blamed Soviet expansionism: Stalin’s takeover of Eastern Europe and his hostile ideology made the Cold War inevitable. Early Cold War historians such as Arthur Schlesinger Jr. held this view.

From the 1960s, revisionist historians such as William Appleman Williams shifted emphasis toward American responsibility, arguing that US economic expansionism — the “Open Door” policy — and atomic diplomacy provoked Soviet defensiveness rather than Soviet aggression causing the conflict. The Vietnam War and revelations about CIA activities deepened public receptiveness to this reading.

Key Fact

The post-revisionist school, developed by John Lewis Gaddis from the 1970s, rejected simple blame narratives. Gaddis argued that both superpowers pursued their own interests and that the Cold War arose from their interaction, not from one side’s aggression alone. Post-Cold War access to Soviet archives from the 1990s gave historians new evidence that largely supported post-revisionist conclusions.

The interpretation of appeasement has also shifted across three schools. The Guilty Men reading, originating in Michael Foot’s 1940 pamphlet, condemned Chamberlain and other appeasers as culpably naive men who handed Hitler advantage after advantage. A.J.P. Taylor’s revisionist approach in “The Origins of the Second World War” (1961) argued that appeasement reflected the genuine popular desire to avoid another catastrophic war — the “Popular Majority” view. More recent revisionist work by R.A.C. Parker argued that Chamberlain had genuine strategic alternatives that he refused to explore, making appeasement a deliberate choice rather than an inevitable response to public pressure.

Examiners reward students who can name these schools and anchor each to specific evidence: for Guilty Men, the Munich Agreement and Chamberlain’s claim of “peace for our time”; for the Popular Majority reading, public opinion polls of 1938; for the Parker revisionist reading, the rejected Soviet alliance proposals of 1939. Quoting a phrase from a given interpretation and linking it to one of these schools is the key technique for the highest band.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers material that appears in the interpretation questions — the highest-value questions on this paper. When evaluating a historical interpretation, the top band requires you to quote a phrase from the extract and link it explicitly to a named school (e.g. “this reflects the orthodox school because...”). For the Cold War, know orthodox (Soviet blame), revisionist (US blame), and post-revisionist (mutual interaction, Gaddis). For Appeasement, know Guilty Men (Foot), Popular Majority (Taylor), and Parker revisionist. Examiners specifically reward students who can name these schools — do not write “some historians think” when you can name Gaddis or Williams.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War; the defeat damaged US credibility and led to the 1973 War Powers Act limiting presidential authority to deploy forces without Congress.
  • Détente (1969–1979) brought SALT I (1972), Nixon’s opening of China, and the Helsinki Accords (1975), but ended when the USSR invaded Afghanistan in December 1979.
  • Cold War historiography has three main schools: orthodox (Soviet blame, 1950s), revisionist (US blame, Williams 1960s), and post-revisionist (mutual interaction, Gaddis 1970s onwards) — post-Cold War Soviet archives broadly supported the post-revisionist reading.

practice_questions.text: Outline two consequences of the fall of Saigon in 1975 for the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed consequences with specific detail (e.g. 58,000 Americans dead; War Powers Act passed; damaged US credibility in Cold War). Secure: Two consequences with some development. Developing: Two consequences identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two features of the policy of détente in the period 1969–1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed features with specific evidence (SALT I 1972 freezing missile numbers; Nixon's 1972 China visit exploiting Sino-Soviet split; Helsinki Accords 1975). Secure: Two features with supporting detail. Developing: Two features identified but development limited. Emerging: One basic point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how interpretations of the origins of the Cold War have changed over time.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated comparison of named schools (orthodox, revisionist, post-revisionist) with named historians (Schlesinger, Williams, Gaddis), specific evidence for each, and an analysis of what changed each school's thinking. Secure: Clear comparison with named schools and some specific evidence. Developing: Two views identified but not developed as a comparative analysis. Emerging: Descriptive account of one viewpoint.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of SALT I signed in May 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. froze numbers of ICBMs; first treaty to limit nuclear weapons growth). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the policy of détente broke down by 1979.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (structural weakness of détente based on negotiation not shared values; Soviet invasion of Afghanistan December 1979; US withdrawal of SALT II) with causal analysis. Secure: Two causes with relevant evidence. Developing: One developed or two briefly stated. Emerging: Simple descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the USA was mainly responsible for the origins of the Cold War? Use your knowledge and the interpretations in this lesson to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument evaluating all three historical schools with named historians and specific evidence; weighs the revisionist claim against orthodox and post-revisionist counter-evidence; reaches a sustained and supported judgement. SPaG: accurate spelling and grammar, consistent use of historical terminology. Secure: Clear argument with named schools and evidence; judgement present but less fully developed. Developing: Some argument referencing two viewpoints; limited use of specific evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account of one viewpoint only.

knowledge_checks.q: On which date did Saigon fall to North Vietnamese forces?
Which historian is most associated with the post-revisionist school of Cold War historiography?
The period of relaxed superpower tensions from roughly 1969 to 1979 was known as _____.
The SALT I agreement, signed in May 1972, froze the number of _____ held by each superpower.
Match each Cold War historical school to its key argument:
right: Both superpowers pursued their interests — the Cold War arose from their interaction
Soviet expansionism and Stalin's aggression made the Cold War inevitable
US economic imperialism and atomic diplomacy provoked Soviet defensiveness

flashcard_questions.a: 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War and unifying Vietnam under communist rule.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the War Powers Act (1973)?
flashcard_questions.a: US law requiring the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and limiting deployments to 60 days without congressional approval.
The policy of managing rather than winning the Cold War through negotiation, c.1969–1979.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Nixon achieve by visiting China in February 1972?
flashcard_questions.a: He opened US diplomatic relations with China, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split to put pressure on the USSR.
The first treaty to limit nuclear weapons, freezing the number of ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles held by each superpower.
Agreements signed by 35 nations recognising existing European borders and including a human rights commitment Soviet dissidents later used against the Kremlin.
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979, triggering a US boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the orthodox school of Cold War historiography?
flashcard_questions.a: The view that Soviet expansionism and Stalin's aggression caused the Cold War; dominant in the 1950s.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is William Appleman Williams and what did he argue?
flashcard_questions.a: American revisionist historian who argued US economic expansionism and the Open Door policy drove Cold War confrontation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the post-revisionist view of the Cold War?
flashcard_questions.a: John Lewis Gaddis argued both superpowers pursued their interests and the Cold War arose from their interaction, not one side's aggression alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'Guilty Men' interpretation of appeasement?
flashcard_questions.a: Michael Foot's 1940 view that Chamberlain and other appeasers were culpably naive in handing Hitler concession after concession.

flashcard_questions.q: What did post-Cold War Soviet archive openings reveal about Cold War historiography?
flashcard_questions.a: New evidence broadly supported the post-revisionist view that both sides bore responsibility for the Cold War.

glossary_terms.definition: The capital of South Vietnam, which fell to North Vietnamese forces on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War and unifying Vietnam under communist rule.
The period of relaxed superpower tensions from roughly 1969 to 1979, characterised by arms control negotiations and reduced Cold War confrontation.
US National Security Adviser and Secretary of State who, with Nixon, pursued détente: managing superpower competition through negotiation rather than confrontation.
Soviet leader 1964–1982 who negotiated the SALT I agreement with Nixon and the Helsinki Accords of 1975 as part of the détente era.
The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks treaty signed in May 1972, freezing the number of ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles held by each superpower.
Agreements signed in 1975 by 35 nations including the USA and USSR, recognising existing European borders and including a human rights commitment.
The Cold War historical school, dominant in the 1950s, that blamed Soviet expansionism and Stalin's aggression for causing the Cold War.
The Cold War historical school from the 1960s that shifted blame toward the United States, arguing US economic imperialism provoked Soviet defensiveness.
American revisionist historian who argued in 'The Tragedy of American Diplomacy' (1959) that US economic expansionism drove Cold War confrontation.
American post-revisionist historian who argued both superpowers pursued their interests and that the Cold War arose from their interaction rather than one side's aggression.
The critique of British appeasement, originating in Michael Foot's 1940 pamphlet, condemning Chamberlain and others as culpably naive in appeasing Hitler.
